messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is an 18-year-old African American police officer who came to treatment exhausted by the sense that he is living braced for something terrible. When he describes where this began, he goes back to childhood nights in a small apartment where he would hear his mother’s boyfriend moving through the rooms before the violence started. What stayed with him are not long, coherent memories but a set of frozen pictures: the boyfriend standing in the hallway, his mother cornered near the kitchen, a hand grabbing, the charged stillness just before shouting and blows. He remembers his own body wedged behind a doorway, muscles locked, trying not to make a sound. Even now, when those moments come back, his body pulls into that same tight, crouched position before he has fully realized what he is remembering, and the memory is accompanied by a crushing grief for his mother and for the boy he was then, unable to stop what was happening.

Over time, Kwame had come to believe that those reactions said something deeply wrong about him. He was certain he should have been able to do more, even as a child, and now he takes his own startle, tension, and mental replaying as evidence that he cannot rely on himself. He worries that the force of these reactions means he is going crazy. Because he feels helpless in the face of danger, he approaches the world as if bad things are always about to break through if he lets his guard down. He avoids unfamiliar places because not already knowing the layout feels intolerable; he says he needs to be able to assess exits, objects, and who is present. Silence is especially hard for him. If a room goes unusually quiet, his whole body reads it as the kind of hush that used to come before violence, and he immediately starts scanning for anything that could be used as a weapon.

Those scans are not abstract. At work, when he enters a home on a call or even steps into a break room he has not used before, his eyes go first to knives, heavy tools, glass objects, anything that could become dangerous. If someone moves in a way he reads as suspicious, or if a person comes up behind him and touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he feels a jolt of raw discomfort that is out of proportion to the moment but completely convincing to him. Those moments pull the old pictures forward. An unexpected touch can bring back the image of a hand grabbing in the hallway; a tense, watchful person can instantly call up the snapshot of his mother’s boyfriend before an assault. The triggers feel potent partly because he has come to expect threat in them, and the more he watches for suspicious behavior or the wrong kind of silence, the more readily ordinary moments seem to match the old scenes.

Once the memories are stirred, they intensify everything else. He feels himself physically pulled back into the posture of hiding and waiting, and that bodily reenactment makes the present environment seem dangerous, not just reminiscent. After a memory surge, he becomes even more vigilant, more convinced that silence signals imminent harm, more fixated on locating possible weapons around him. The memories also deepen his beliefs about himself. If a few sensory details can overtake him that completely, he takes it as proof that he is not in control of his own mind and cannot depend on himself under pressure. What frightens him most is not only the memory itself but the idea that having it means he is losing his sanity.

That interpretation, in turn, makes the next trigger more likely. Because he is already judging his reactions as intolerable and incomprehensible, even mild discomfort in public feels dangerous. He watches himself so closely that suspicious behavior in others, unfamiliar settings, and unprepared touch all become loaded before anything has actually happened. Then the environment starts to narrow around him. He keeps to familiar routes, arrives early so he can study a room, and stays tense in quiet moments on shift because the absence of noise feels like the prelude to an attack. The more he lives that way, the more his mind stays organized around those childhood images, and the more easily they return.

By the time he sought help, the strain was affecting both work and the little life he keeps outside it. He is single and increasingly withdrawn, choosing predictability over seeing people or going anywhere new. What finally brought him in was the fear that one day an unexpected touch or a suspicious movement on the job would flood him so completely with those old pictures that he would stop trusting his own judgment altogether. More than anything, Kwame wants to know whether he can learn to feel safe without having to stay on guard every second, and whether these reactions mean he is damaged beyond repair.
